section.title: Judgment on Israel and Judah
section.sectionRationale: The lawsuit of chapter 4 widens. Now priests, people, and the royal house are all summoned, and Judah is named alongside Israel. The chapter exposes a nation that will bring its flocks to seek the LORD but cannot find Him, because its heart never turned, and that runs to Assyria for the healing only God can give.
section.thesis: Because a spirit of prostitution keeps Israel and Judah from truly knowing the LORD, God withdraws His felt presence and becomes to them like a moth and then a lion, until at last, broken by affliction, they admit their guilt and seek His face.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the summons and snare that entrap the whole nation; the deeds that bar the way back to God; and the LORD who wounds like a lion yet withdraws so that they will seek Him.

units.label: The summons and the snare
units.note: priests, people, and palace all charged

verses.text: “Hear this, O priests! Take heed, O house of Israel! Give ear, O royal house! For this judgment is against you because you have been a snare at Mizpah, a net spread out on Tabor.
The rebels are deep in slaughter; but I will chastise them all.
I know all about Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from Me. For now, O Ephraim, you have turned to {{zenunim|prostitution}}; Israel is defiled.

units.label: Deeds that bar the way back
units.note: they do not know the LORD

verses.text: Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God, for a spirit of {{zenunim|prostitution}} is within them, and they do not {{yada|know}} the LORD.
Israel’s arrogance testifies against them; Israel and Ephraim stumble in their iniquity; even Judah stumbles with them.
They go with their flocks and herds to seek the LORD, but they do not find Him; He has withdrawn Himself from them.
They have been unfaithful to the LORD; for they have borne illegitimate children. Now the New Moon will devour them along with their land.

units.label: The alarm and the moth
units.note: war on the horizon, decay within

verses.text: Blow the ram’s horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah; raise the battle cry in Beth-aven: Lead on, O Benjamin!
Ephraim will be laid waste on the day of rebuke. Among the tribes of Israel I proclaim what is certain.
The princes of Judah are like those who move boundary stones; I will pour out My fury upon them like water.
Ephraim is oppressed, crushed in judgment, for he is determined to follow worthless idols.
So I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like decay to the house of Judah.

units.label: The lion who withdraws until they seek His face

verses.text: When Ephraim saw his sickness and Judah his wound, then Ephraim turned to Assyria and sent to the great king. But he cannot cure you or heal your wound.
For I am like a lion to Ephraim and like a young lion to the house of Judah. I, even I, will tear them to pieces and then go away. I will carry them off where no one can rescue them.
Then I will return to My place until they {{asham|admit their guilt}} and seek My face; in their affliction they will earnestly seek Me.”

zenunim.gloss: Prostitution, promiscuity, harlotry. In Hosea it is the standing image for Israel's covenant unfaithfulness, chasing other gods and other nations as a wife chases lovers. Here it names a settled disposition, a spirit of prostitution that lives within the people and steers them away from the LORD.

yada.gloss: To know, in the deep, relational sense of intimate acquaintance, not mere information. In Hosea to know the LORD is to live in loyal covenant fellowship with Him. Israel's failure to know Him, the same lack named in chapter 4, is the root of the ruin here.

asham.gloss: To be guilty, to bear guilt, to acknowledge one's guilt. The word can carry the whole movement from being guilty to owning it. In verse 15 God waits until Israel stops excusing itself and confesses its guilt, the turning point that opens the way back to Him.

basic.context: The court case widens to include the priests, the ordinary people, and the king's household, and even Judah is drawn in. Israel is so entangled in unfaithfulness that its very deeds keep it from returning to God. The people still bring animals to sacrifice, but they cannot find the LORD, because their hearts never turned. When they feel the wound of coming judgment, they run to Assyria for help instead of to God. So the LORD becomes like a moth quietly eating them away, then like a lion, and finally He withdraws, waiting for the day affliction drives them to seek His face.
basic.hermeneutics: This is still covenant lawsuit, moving from summons to sentence. The heaping up of place names, Mizpah, Tabor, Gibeah, Ramah, Beth-aven, roots the charges in real Israelite worship centers and battle lines. God's withdrawal is not caprice; it is measured discipline aimed at repentance, as the last verse makes plain.
basic.originalLanguages: A spirit of zenunim, prostitution, lives within the people and blocks their return. The fatal lack is again that they do not yada, know, the LORD, an intimate covenant knowing. The hope hangs on one word in the final verse, asham, to admit guilt: God waits until Israel owns its guilt and seeks His face.
basic.typology: The incurable wound that Assyria's king could not heal points to the deeper sickness of sin that no earthly power can cure, answered only in Christ the Great Physician. God's withdrawal until His people seek His face foreshadows the pattern of the gospel, where affliction drives sinners to seek and find Him in Christ.
basic.christ: Israel's wound had no cure in Assyria, and no political alliance can heal the sickness of sin. Jesus is the Physician who came for the sick, who bears our wounds and by His stripes heals us. Where God withdrew until His people would seek His face, Christ is the face of God turned toward sinners; in Him the seeking heart truly finds the LORD.
basic.god: God knows His people completely, nothing is hidden from Him. He is patient but not indulgent: He will discipline like a moth and a lion rather than leave sin to fester. Yet even His withdrawal is purposeful mercy, designed to bring a proud people to the end of themselves so they will admit their guilt and seek Him.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 9:12 shows Jesus as the Physician of the sick. Deuteronomy 31:17 warns that God will hide His face when His people forsake Him. 2 Chronicles 7:14 promises that if His people humble themselves and seek His face, He will heal.
basic.oneStory: Chapter 5 shows a people who seek God with sacrifices but never with their hearts, and cannot find Him. The whole Bible answers that impasse in Christ, in whom God turns His face toward sinners and the seeking heart at last finds the God it lost.

context.literary:
Hosea 5 is the sharpest turn so far in a book that began with a marriage. Chapters 1 to 3 told the story of Hosea and Gomer, and chapter 4 opened the courtroom: the LORD 'has a case against the people of the land,' Hosea 4:1. Chapter 5 now calls the defendants by name and passes sentence, and it does so in two movements. Verses 1 to 7 are summons and charge. Three groups are called to attention in descending order of responsibility, priests, then the house of Israel, then the royal house, and the diagnosis arrives in verse 4 as an inner condition rather than a list of deeds. Verses 8 to 15 are sentence, and they read like a dispatch from a war: alarm horns in verse 8, a sure verdict in verse 9, a rebuke of Judah's rulers in verse 10, and then a run of savage images that end in a quiet withdrawal.

Notice how the speaking voice changes. The first verses are the prophet calling on God's behalf, but from verse 12 God speaks in the first person almost without pause: 'I am like a moth,' 'I am like a lion,' 'I, even I, will tear them to pieces.' The pronoun doubles in verse 14, and by verse 15 God is the only actor left in the scene. Israel's own busy activity, flocks and herds, alliances, messengers to a king, is answered by a God who simply does something.

Two refrains tie the chapter into the wider book. 'Israel's arrogance testifies against them' in verse 5 comes back word for word in Hosea 7:10. And the stumbling of verse 5, which spreads from Israel and Ephraim to Judah, reaches forward to the closing appeal, 'you have stumbled by your iniquity,' Hosea 14:1. The chapter ends on an open door. The final verse is not a closing sentence but a condition, 'until they admit their guilt and seek My face,' and the next chapter begins with a song that sounds as if the people had heard it.
context.historical:
Hosea's ministry is dated in Hosea 1:1 to the reigns of Jeroboam II in the north and four kings in Judah, but this chapter belongs to the troubled years after Jeroboam's death. Assyria was now a looming power. Menahem of Israel bought off its king, Pul, with a thousand talents of silver, raised by a levy of fifty shekels on each wealthy man, 2 Kings 15:19-20. Later Pekah of Israel joined Rezin of Aram in a war against Judah, 2 Kings 16:5, and Ahaz of Judah answered by sending messengers to Tiglath-pileser with the words 'I am your servant and your son,' 2 Kings 16:7. Many readers place verses 8 to 14 in that setting, and the 'great king' of verse 13 fits it. Tiglath-pileser did come, but he stripped Israel of Gilead, Galilee and the land of Naphtali, 2 Kings 15:29, and he was no healer of anyone.

The place names are chosen with care. Gibeah and Ramah lay on the border road in Benjamin north of Jerusalem, where the two kingdoms met. Beth-aven, 'house of wickedness,' is Hosea's bitter nickname for Bethel, 'house of God,' where Jeroboam I had set up a golden calf, 1 Kings 12:28-29. Mizpah and Tabor name two well known high places, and the language of 'snare' and 'net' is the language of a bird catcher. The picture is of the leadership setting traps for the very people they should have shepherded.

Verse 10 would have struck a Judean ear painfully. Moving a boundary stone was a crime against the family inheritance, Deuteronomy 19:14, and it was a sin the wise warned against, Proverbs 22:28. Land grabbing by powerful men was never only an Israelite fault. The New Moon of verse 7 was a monthly sacred day with its own offerings, Numbers 28:11-15, so the judgment lands in the middle of their calendar of worship.
context.canonical:
Hosea 5 draws on the covenant lawsuit, the form in which God summons His people before heaven and earth to answer for broken promises, as in Deuteronomy 32, Isaiah 1:2-3 and Micah 6:1-2. Its sentence is built from the covenant's own warnings. The withdrawal of verse 15 is the hiding of God's face threatened in Deuteronomy 31:17-18, and the unfindable God of verse 6 is the grim mirror of Deuteronomy 4:29, where Israel is promised that those who seek with all their heart will find. Isaiah later says the same thing in prose: 'your sins have hidden His face from you,' Isaiah 59:2.

The images of verses 12 to 14 are taken up elsewhere. The lion who tears and goes away returns in Hosea 13:7-8, and Amos says the lion has roared and asks who will not fear, Amos 3:8. The incurable wound is Isaiah's portrait of the nation from head to foot, Isaiah 1:5-6, and Jeremiah's, 'Your injury is incurable,' Jeremiah 30:12, but Jeremiah goes on to the answer Hosea is preparing: 'I will restore your health and heal your wounds,' Jeremiah 30:17. Hosea himself supplies the reply almost at once, since the next three verses are the people's own promise that the one who tore will heal, Hosea 6:1.

In the New Testament the pattern of affliction that drives a person to seek is not quoted from this chapter, but it is lived out by the younger son who 'came to his senses' in a far country, Luke 15:17, and it is taught by Hebrews, where the Father's discipline 'yields a harvest of righteousness and peace,' Hebrews 12:11. Most of all, Jesus describes Himself as the physician for the sick, Matthew 9:12, and as the one who came 'to seek and to save the lost,' Luke 19:10, which is the very reverse of a God who goes to His place and waits.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Hosea wanted his hearers to lose a comfortable belief: that the worst danger to a nation is outside it. The accused in this chapter are the priests, who should have taught the knowledge of God, and the royal house, who should have guarded justice. When the people's guides are the snare, ordinary people are caught in a net they did not see. He wanted the leaders especially to feel that being in office is not a shield but an accountability.

He wanted them to understand the kind of problem they had. Verse 4 says their deeds 'do not permit' them to return, because 'a spirit of prostitution is within them.' The trouble is not that God has closed the door but that the habits of a heart bent toward other lovers have made the door seem pointless. A person can be too accustomed to evasion to turn. That is a frightening claim, and Hosea means it to be.

He wanted them to see their political cleverness as a form of unfaith. Sending to Assyria was ordinary statecraft, and a careful statesman might have defended it. Hosea names it for what it was, a decision to seek healing from the one who was himself the next threat, while ignoring the One who had struck the wound.

And he wanted the last verse heard. God's retreat is not abandonment. The sentence has an end built into it: a time when affliction makes them 'admit their guilt and seek My face.' A hearer who took that seriously would not wait for the lion but would go and seek the LORD while the moth was still at work.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes how Israel behaved and how God judged them in one historical moment. It does not hand believers a table by which every disaster can be traced back to a particular sin. Jesus Himself warns against that move when He says of a man born blind, 'Neither this man nor his parents sinned,' John 9:3. The moth and the lion are pictures of God's judgment on a covenant nation that had been warned, not a formula for reading a nation's troubles today, and certainly not for reading one person's suffering.

What carries over is the pattern. God holds those who lead especially responsible, which is why James says teachers 'will be judged more strictly,' James 3:1. A people can go through the motions of worship while their hearts are elsewhere, which is why verse 6 is not a model but a warning: they sacrifice and cannot find Him. And the instinct to run to a powerful helper before running to God is a standing temptation for individuals as much as for kings, as Isaiah warns, 'they do not look to the Holy One of Israel,' Isaiah 31:1.

The final verse is the part to take as promise. Where God hides His face, He does so with an end in view, and the way to meet affliction is to seek Him, not to carry on as before.

debates.question: What are the horns of verse 8 announcing, and who is attacking whom?

views.label: An Israelite attack on Judah in the Syro-Ephraimite war
views.case: Gibeah and Ramah lay just inside Judah's border region of Benjamin, and 2 Kings 16:5 tells how Pekah and Rezin marched on Jerusalem. Verse 10 then rebukes the princes of Judah, and Judah is mentioned throughout the chapter. On this reading the alarm is Judah's, or the call to Benjamin to resist a northern advance.

views.label: A prophetic warning of the Assyrian invasion
views.case: Others hear the horns as the alarm of an invader who has not yet arrived. The horn is the standard watchman's signal in Hosea 8:1 and in Amos 3:6, and verse 9 says Ephraim 'will be laid waste on the day of rebuke,' which speaks of a coming verdict, not a battle already under way.

views.label: A summons to arms by Ephraim against Judah's land grabbing
views.case: A third reading connects verse 8 with verse 10: Judah's princes have moved boundary stones, and the horns call Benjamin out against them. This keeps the border imagery and explains why Judah is judged by name.

debates.bearing: The text names places and not a date, and honest readers differ. The theological point stands under every reading: God proclaims 'what is certain' among the tribes, verse 9, and both kingdoms are within His reach.

debates.question: What does 'the New Moon will devour them' mean in verse 7?

views.label: The festival itself becomes the occasion of judgment
views.case: The monthly feast, a high point of the calendar, Numbers 28:11, is the very time when judgment comes. Their worship does not protect them from the sentence; it is the setting of it. Isaiah says something close: 'your New Moons, Sabbaths, and convocations. I cannot endure iniquity in a solemn assembly,' Isaiah 1:13.

views.label: A short period of time
views.case: The word for new moon is also the word for month. The BSB footnote offers 'the coming month.' On this reading the threat is that within a month the land and its people will be consumed, a warning with a deadline.

views.label: The feast of the new moon as an act of devouring
views.case: A few read the verb as the devouring that the feast itself accomplishes, that their celebration eats them up spiritually, because it is offered to the wrong God or in the wrong heart.

debates.bearing: The first two views are both possible and not far apart: whether it is the feast or the month, the point is that Israel's religious calendar offers no protection when the heart has turned away, which is what verse 6 has already said.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 5 says Israel's 'arrogance' testifies against them. The noun is gaon, the word for pride or majesty, and it has two edges in the Old Testament: it can be the glory of a thing, and it can be the swagger of a person. Here it is the second. The way it testifies is by being visible, since the verb carries the sense of answering a charge, so that their own bearing gives the evidence. The same sentence returns in Hosea 7:10, a sign that it was worth saying twice.

Verse 7 says they 'have been unfaithful.' The verb is bagad, to act treacherously, and it is the word for a faithless spouse in Jeremiah 3:20, 'as a woman may betray her husband, so you have betrayed Me, O house of Israel.' The marriage imagery of chapters 1 to 3 is carried into the courtroom by a single verb.

In verse 12 the BSB has 'moth' and 'decay.' The first is ash, the clothes moth, whose damage is silent and slow. The second is rakav, which names rot, the word used of 'rottenness' in the bones in Proverbs 14:30, a process that works inside and shows late. Together they describe God's judgment as something more quiet than war. The nation is being eaten from within before the lion is ever mentioned.

Verses 14 and 15 are joined by a sound as well as a sense. 'I will tear them to pieces' uses the verb taraf, the word for what a beast does to prey. When the people sing in Hosea 6:1, 'He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us,' they use the same verb. They have understood whose teeth have been at them. The 'young lion,' kephir, is a lion in its prime, strong enough to hunt for itself.

The last verse has two verbs for seeking. The first is the ordinary biqqesh, to look for. The second, rendered 'earnestly seek,' is related to shachar, the dawn, and so carries the idea of seeking early and eagerly, as in Psalm 63:1, 'Earnestly I seek You.' The people had sought with flocks and herds, verse 6, which is a sacrifice in search of an audience. God asks for a search with the face turned toward Him.

Finally, verse 11 is an example of a text translators do not agree on. The BSB has 'worthless idols,' while a footnote offers 'human precepts.' The Hebrew word is rare. Either way Ephraim follows what someone has commanded other than the LORD.

typology.type: The wound no king can cure, verse 13
typology.fulfillment: Ephraim sees his sickness and sends to the great king, but 'he cannot cure you or heal your wound.' Isaiah describes the same condition as a body without a sound place from head to foot, Isaiah 1:5-6. The correspondence in Christ is exact and surprising: the healing comes through another's wounding, 'by His stripes we are healed,' Isaiah 53:5, and Peter applies it to the cross, 1 Peter 2:24. Matthew sees Jesus' healing ministry as the carrying of diseases, Matthew 8:17. The type falls short in one respect: Assyria could only offer protection against an enemy, while Christ deals with the condition itself, sin.

typology.type: The hiding of God's face until they seek, verse 15
typology.fulfillment: The curse of Deuteronomy 31:17-18 comes to rest in Israel as an absence. In the cross the absence is borne by a substitute. Jesus cries, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' Matthew 27:46, and the veil of the sanctuary is torn, Matthew 27:51. He enters the hiddenness so that no one who comes through Him need wait for God to return to His place. The escalation is complete: Israel's withdrawal was earned by its own guilt, His was borne for the guilt of others. Paul says He was made a curse for us, Galatians 3:13. The type does not reach as far as the One who finds the lost; here God only waits.

typology.type: The lion who tears and goes away, verse 14
typology.fulfillment: The lion is an image of judgment, and in Hosea it is God. In Revelation the title belongs to Christ, 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah,' who has triumphed, and who then appears as a Lamb that was slain, Revelation 5:5-6. The same strength that tears in judgment is the strength that conquers for His people. The pattern is not a code for every detail of Hosea's lion, and it would be wrong to read Jesus into the tearing of Israel. But the Bible's own use of the image shows that the one who judges is the one who redeems, and that He bears the cost Himself.

typology.type: Sacrifice offered without finding God, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: Flocks and herds were brought to seek the LORD, and He was not found. Hebrews explains why sacrifice of animals could not be enough: 'it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins,' Hebrews 10:4. Christ offered Himself 'once for all,' Hebrews 7:27, and entered the Most Holy Place 'by His own blood,' Hebrews 9:12. The escalation is from a sacrifice that cannot reach God to one that brings God to us. The type breaks down because the law's sacrifices were commanded by God and were not wrong in themselves. What failed in Hosea's day was not the altar but the heart that came to it.

study.christ:
Hosea 5 leads to Christ by contrast first of all. Israel is sick and goes to the wrong physician. The prophet's complaint, 'he cannot cure you or heal your wound,' sets a question that the Gospels answer in the person of Jesus. When the Pharisees object to His table, He says, 'It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick,' Matthew 9:12, and He quotes Hosea 6:6 in the same breath. The Physician is the One whom the whole nation had passed by.

It leads to Him by pattern in the matter of God's face. The sentence of verse 15, 'I will return to My place until they admit their guilt and seek My face,' describes a God who stays away until the people come. The Gospels tell of a God who does the opposite. 'The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost,' Luke 19:10. He does not stay in His place; He leaves it, takes flesh and goes to where the sick are. At the cross He enters the very absence that this chapter threatens. 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' is the cry of the One who takes into Himself the withdrawal that Israel had earned, Matthew 27:46. The veil is torn from top to bottom, and the way to the face of God, which Isaiah said sin had hidden, Isaiah 59:2, is opened.

It leads to Him by the theme of tearing and healing. The verb of verse 14, 'I will tear,' becomes the people's confession in Hosea 6:1, and the One who is torn most is the Servant, who 'was pierced for our transgressions,' Isaiah 53:5. The wounding of the cross and the healing of the church are the same event. Peter writes, 'By His stripes you are healed,' 1 Peter 2:24.

It leads to Him, lastly, by the contrast of kingship. Israel's rulers send to a foreign king for help and discover that he is no healer. The true King does not send. He comes Himself, and He deals with the disease at its root.

A caution keeps this honest. The moth and the lion in verses 12 to 14 are images of divine judgment, not coded pictures of Jesus, and Hosea does not name a coming Physician. What the chapter supplies is the diagnosis and the unhealed wound, and it states with unusual clarity what Israel and every later reader needed: a healer from outside the circle of the sick, and a seeking that is answered. The New Testament says that He has come.
study.god:
The chapter first shows a God who knows. 'I know all about Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from Me,' verse 3. Israel's attempt to find Him with flocks and herds fails, verse 6, but His knowledge of them does not fail at all. Nothing in their religion or their politics is out of His sight. That is a comfort to the honest and a terror to the pretender.

He is just in an ordered way. The charge comes first, in verses 1 to 7, and only then the sentence. The punishment is also proportioned to the offence: those who made themselves a snare are snared, and those who sought help from Assyria are given Assyria. God's justice here is not an outburst of temper but the working out of covenant terms to which He had committed Himself and warned about in advance.

He is a God who acts by withdrawing. The moth and the lion are active, but the last move is to leave. Hiddenness is one of the strangest forms of God's work in the Bible, and Hosea presents it as a deliberate act, 'I will return to My place.' It is a way of telling a people that the God they have been using is a God who can be missed. There is a fierce tenderness in that: He will take away the thing they have taken for granted until they ask for it.

He is jealous in the sense of a covenant Husband. The language of unfaithfulness in verse 7 and prostitution in verses 3 and 4 is the speech of a wronged lover, not an offended magistrate. Hosea does not allow a split between God's justice and His love; the sentence is itself shaped by love, as verse 15 shows.

He is sovereign over the nations. Assyria is a tool and not a rival, and the 'great king' who looks like a possible saviour has no power to cure. God declares in verse 14 that He Himself will carry them off 'where no one can rescue them.'

There is a tension the chapter does not resolve: the same God who tears is the God who will receive them back. Hosea 6:1 turns that tension into a song, and Hosea 11:8 into a cry of the divine heart. For worship, the chapter teaches that the way to meet God is not to bring more and larger offerings but to turn the face toward Him, to say what is true about ourselves, and to seek Him early, while there is still a chance of finding Him near.

crossReferences.note: The warning behind verse 15. God says He will hide His face when His people forsake Him and go after other gods, and that on that day many troubles will come on them. Hosea shows the sentence in operation, and the hiding is not the end of the story, since the next verses of Deuteronomy 31 give Israel a song to remember.

The promise that seems reversed in Hosea 5:6. From exile they will seek the LORD and find Him if they seek with all their heart and soul. Hosea shows what fails: they seek with flocks and herds, not with the heart, so they do not find. The two passages show the condition on which finding depends.

Menahem pays Pul of Assyria a thousand talents of silver, raised by a levy on every wealthy man. This is the history behind 'Ephraim turned to Assyria' in verse 13. It is a record of a king who purchased protection and found that it came with a cost to his own people.

Pekah and Rezin besiege Ahaz in Jerusalem, and Ahaz sends gold and silver to Tiglath-pileser asking to be saved. Judah is guilty of the same reflex as Ephraim, which is why Hosea says the wound is Judah's too, verse 13. Assyria took the money, and Judah was not healed.

The proverb that stands behind verse 10: 'Do not move an ancient boundary stone which your fathers have placed.' The princes of Judah are accused of treating what God had apportioned as theirs to shift. The sin is old, and so is the wisdom, which is why the footnote in the BSB points here.

A sister portrait of national sickness: a whole head sore and a whole heart faint, wounds never bandaged or softened with oil. Isaiah, Hosea's contemporary, shows the same disease from Jerusalem's side, and he too asks why they want more beatings, which is what happens when the wrong cure is sought.

Where Hosea says that Assyria cannot heal, Jeremiah starts with the same incurable wound and then answers with God's own promise to restore health and heal wounds. It shows that the failure of every other physician is not the end of hope but the setting for His own work.

The people's reply to the closing verse of chapter 5, using the same verb for tearing and the same word for healing. Reading the two chapters together shows that the sentence in 5:15 was meant to produce just such a song, and chapter 6 then tests whether the song is true.

The prodigal 'came to his senses' in a far country, and then rose to go to his father. It is not a fulfilment of Hosea 5:15, but it shows what God's withdrawal aims at: a seeking that begins when affliction strips away the excuses. In Luke the father is already looking down the road.

Jesus' cry from the cross takes up the language of God's hidden face. The One who knew the Father perfectly entered the experience that Hosea 5:15 describes for a guilty people, so that those who seek Him through the Son need not be left to look in vain.

The end of the story reverses chapter 5. The tree of life has leaves 'for the healing of the nations,' there is no longer any curse, and God's servants 'will see His face.' The wound is healed and the face that was withdrawn is seen.

study.oneStory:
The question of Hosea 5 is the oldest in the Bible: what happens when those who were made for God's presence turn to other lovers? Genesis 3 had answered with exile and a cherub at the gate. Israel's whole history after Sinai repeats the pattern in small. Under Joshua and the judges, a people bring on themselves an oppressor, cry out, and are given a deliverer, as in Judges 3:9. Hosea's contemporaries are in the last act of that cycle, and the difference now is that the oppressor is not an occasional raiding party but an empire, and the people are no longer crying out to the LORD.

The chapter looks back to the covenant at Sinai and its sanctions. The hiding of God's face, the sword, the beasts and the exile, all of which Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 to 32 had foretold, now begin to arrive. It is a moment when God is shown to keep His word even when the word is a warning. The northern kingdom would fall to Assyria after a siege of three years, 2 Kings 17:5, and its people would be taken away, as 2 Kings 17:7-23 explains by reference to the same sins.

The chapter looks forward in two directions. First, it points to the exile of Judah, which Hosea's 'even Judah stumbles with them' already anticipates, and it sets up the great prophetic hope that the same God who wounds will bind up. Second, it points to the cross. At the cross God's withdrawal is borne, not by the guilty but by the one who took their guilt, and the cry of forsakenness is heard on behalf of those who would otherwise never find Him.

The Bible ends where Hosea 5 begins to point. 'They will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. The face that was hidden is finally seen. The tree of life, which Genesis 3 blocked, stands in the city with leaves for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2, and there is no longer any curse, Revelation 22:3. Every attempt to find healing in the wrong place, the alliance, the sanctuary, the clever policy, is answered by the God who provides the true remedy and brings His people home.

quiz.q: Why can the people not find the LORD even though they bring flocks and herds to seek Him?

options.text: Their hearts never turned; a spirit of prostitution keeps them from truly knowing God, so the ritual is empty.
options.note: Verses 4 and 6 tie their failure to find God to unfaithful hearts, not insufficient offerings.

options.text: They did not bring enough animals to sacrifice.
options.note: The quantity of offerings is not the issue; the absence of a returning heart is.

options.text: They went to the wrong shrine on the wrong day.
options.note: Location and timing are not the problem; their inner unfaithfulness is.

options.text: God had simply stopped existing for them.
options.note: God has withdrawn as discipline, not ceased to be; He waits for them to seek His face.

quiz.q: What does Israel do when it feels the wound of coming judgment?

options.text: It turns to Assyria and the great king for a cure, instead of turning to the LORD.
options.note: Verse 13 shows Ephraim seeking healing from a foreign power that cannot help.

options.text: It immediately repents and admits its guilt.
options.note: True repentance is what God waits for, but here they run to Assyria first.

options.text: It rebuilds the temple in Jerusalem.
options.note: The text describes flight to Assyria, not temple rebuilding.

options.text: It calls a national day of prayer that God accepts.
options.note: Their seeking is hollow; God withdraws rather than accepting it.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of God withdrawing to His place in verse 15?

options.text: To wait until, broken by affliction, they admit their guilt and earnestly seek His face.
options.note: Verse 15 names the goal of the withdrawal: honest confession and seeking.

options.text: To abandon them forever with no hope of return.
options.note: The withdrawal is disciplinary and hopeful, not final abandonment.

options.text: To rest because He was tired of judging.
options.note: God does not withdraw from weariness; He withdraws with a redemptive aim.

options.text: To let another god take His place among them.
options.note: There is no rival to the LORD; He withdraws to draw them back to Himself.

quiz.q: How does the incurable wound point forward to Christ?

options.text: The sickness Assyria could not heal is sin itself, cured only by Christ the Physician who heals by His wounds.
options.note: Jesus comes for the sick and bears our wounds, 1 Peter 2:24.

options.text: It shows that better doctors would have solved the problem.
options.note: The wound is spiritual; no human remedy reaches it, only Christ.

options.text: It predicts the fall of the Assyrian empire.
options.note: The point is the need Christ meets, not a forecast about Assyria.

options.text: It has nothing to do with Christ.
options.note: The incurable wound is exactly the need the gospel answers in Jesus.

quiz.q: What does the movement from moth to lion teach about God's patience?

options.text: God often works slowly and quietly first, but His patience must not be presumed upon, for judgment can come suddenly.
options.note: The moth pictures slow decay; the lion pictures sudden tearing.

options.text: God never acts in judgment at all.
options.note: The lion imagery shows real judgment does come.

options.text: God's patience means sin has no consequences.
options.note: The chapter shows patience alongside certain consequences.

options.text: God is unpredictable and arbitrary in His anger.
options.note: His discipline is measured and purposeful, aimed at repentance.

questions: The people sought God with sacrifices but not with their hearts. Where might your own religious activity be masking a heart that has not truly returned?
Israel ran to Assyria for a cure only God could give. What earthly Assyria do you turn to first when you feel the wound of your sin or trouble?
God withdrew to bring His people to admit their guilt. Is there guilt you have been excusing rather than owning honestly before God?
The wound Assyria could not heal is met in Christ the Physician. What wound do you need to bring to Him rather than to a lesser remedy?
God waits to be sought. What would it look like this week to seek His face in earnest rather than out of routine?

translationNotes.note: The New Moon may also be rendered their New Moon feast or the coming month; either way a set religious time will turn into the occasion of ruin.
Beth-aven, house of wickedness, is a derogatory name for Bethel, house of God, a center of Israel's false worship, as in chapter 4.
Determined to follow worthless idols may also be rendered determined to follow human precepts, following a variant reading of the Hebrew.
The great king may be read as the proper name King Jareb; the sense is the Assyrian monarch to whom Israel appealed for help.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Hosea 5:1-15, with poetic lines joined into running verses.
